headline: Halfway Rock and Bailey Island Ledges Take Over as the Marshes Empty Out
subhead: Striped bass are abandoning Casco Bay's back marshes for river mouths and open-water structure as Harvest Moon tides push bait hard, while cod and haddock hold their depth on the rock.
body_markdown:
Stand on the Peaks Island ferry landing at first light this week and you'll notice something the summer crowd missed: the back marshes behind Peaks and Cousins Island have gone quiet. The peanut bunker and mummichogs that held schoolie bass in those shallow guts through July and August have thinned out, and that's the tell. Casco Bay is making its turn — out of the marsh pattern and into the fall structure game, where river mouths, ledges, and current seams do the work that eelgrass flats did all summer.

The Harvest Moon tides this week are the driver. Bigger swings mean more water moving faster over structure, which means bait gets flushed out of the shallow systems and concentrated where the current squeezes it — off the mouth of the Presumpscot, along the eastern side of Peaks, and out around the open-water ledges like Halfway Rock and the rock piles off Bailey Island. We flagged this two weeks ago, saying the fall run would build and hold strong as the season turned, and that's exactly the shift showing up on the sounders now. Bass are stacking on structure instead of scattering across mudflats.

Halfway Rock remains the most reliable read on the bay right now. The bass are working the edges of the ledge in 25 to 45 feet, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb when the current pulls bait off the rock and funnels it into the deeper water to the south and east. Trolling umbrella rigs and tube-and-worm combinations behind planers has been the steadier producer for boats working that structure, though the fly and light-tackle crowd working the shallower shelf on the north side with 2-ounce white bucktails tipped with a sliver of mackerel belly have connected with fish in the 28- to 34-inch range on the first hour of the incoming, when bait gets pushed up onto the rock instead of off it.

Mackerel are still around, though not in the density of the spring run — expect scattered schools rather than the tight, water-boiling pods that show up in May. When you find them working bird activity off Cape Small or along the Harpswell shoreline, small diamond jigs and Swedish pimples worked with a fast, erratic retrieve in 20 to 35 feet will draw strikes, and where the mackerel concentrate, bluefish have been riding along, chopping through the same schools. Blues in the 3- to 6-pound range have been mixing into the bait balls off Jewell Island and along the outer edge of Bailey Island's ledges, and they'll hit anything moving fast — a 1-ounce Kastmaster or a Hopkins spoon fished on wire leader will save you tackle.

Groundfish are holding their pattern on the deeper structure. Cod and haddock around Halfway Rock and the surrounding ledge complex have been steady rather than spectacular this week — the kind of bite that rewards patience over volume. Jigging with diamond jigs tipped with a piece of clam or squid on the bottom third of the water column, right on the change of the tide when the current slacks enough to hold bottom without excessive scope, has been the more consistent presentation. Boats working the slack water at the top of the tide have done better than those fighting a hard-running current, which makes sense given how tight to bottom these fish are sitting as water temperatures start their seasonal slide.

The honest read: this isn't a blitz week. The bite is real but it's not concentrated into the kind of surface chaos you'll see further south as bunker schools funnel down the coast. Casco Bay's fall run builds more deliberately — bass moving out of the shallows in stages, settling onto structure as the water cools, rather than exploding all at once. That's actually good news for anyone willing to be methodical about it. The fish are there, they're just distributed across a wider stretch of structure than they were mid-summer, and finding them means reading current, not just running to a hot spot from last week.

Looking ahead, the next several days should sharpen this pattern rather than change it. The Harvest Moon tides will keep running big through the weekend, which should keep bait moving and keep concentrating fish on current seams at the top and bottom of the tide. If the wind stays out of the northwest and holds under 15 knots, Halfway Rock and the Bailey Island ledges should fish well on the ebb tide mornings, with the better bass activity likely in the two hours bracketing the tide change. If a cold front pushes through mid-week, as the pattern this time of year often brings, expect the bass bite to intensify further as falling water temperatures push more fish out of the remaining marsh pockets and onto the ledges — but also expect the mackerel schools to thin further as they continue their move offshore and south. Cape Small and the outer Harpswell shoreline are worth checking for that mackerel-bluefish combination before that window closes. For groundfish, the deeper ledge structure around Halfway Rock should remain the more dependable play regardless of what the surface does, since cod and haddock are keying off bottom temperature and current, not the moon.
